Content:
Suppose [MATH: S] is a set. The power set of [MATH: S,] denoted [MATH: \mathcal{P}(S),] is the set containing every subset of [MATH: S,] including the empty set.

Content:
For example, let's find the power set of the set

Content:
[MATH: S = \{ 1,2,3 \}.]

Content:
To do this, we list out all the subsets of [MATH: S{:}]

Content:
- The subset containing no elements is [MATH: \emptyset.]
- The subsets containing [MATH: 1] element are [MATH: \{ 1 \},] [MATH: \{ 2 \},] and [MATH: \{ 3 \}.]
- The subsets containing [MATH: 2] elements are [MATH: \{ 1,2 \},] [MATH: \{ 1,3 \},] and [MATH: \{ 2,3 \}.]
- The subset containing [MATH: 3] elements is [MATH: S] itself: [MATH: \{ 1,2,3 \}.]

Content:
Now, let's put all these subsets together as elements of a single set. We get

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{P}(S) = \big\{ \emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{ 1,2 \}, \{ 1,3 \}, \{ 2,3 \}, \{ 1,2,3 \} \big\}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The power set of [MATH: A,] denoted [MATH: \mathcal{P}(A),] is the set that contains every possible subset of [MATH: A,] including the empty set [MATH: \emptyset.]

So, let's list all possible subsets of [MATH: A] using a tree diagram.

According to our diagram, the subsets of [MATH: A] are [MATH: \emptyset = \{\},\quad \{2\},\quad \{4\},\quad \{ \{8\} \}, \quad \{2, 4\},\quad \{2, \{8\}\},\quad \{4, \{8\}\},\quad\{2, 4, \{8\}\}.]

Therefore, we have [MATH: \mathcal{P}(A) = \{\emptyset, \{2\}, \{4\}, \{\{8\}\}, \{2, 4\}, \{2, \{8\}\}, \{4, \{8\}\},\{2, 4, \{8\}\}\}.]

Content:
Suppose we have a finite set [MATH: S] with cardinality [MATH: |S|.] Then, the cardinality of [MATH: \mathcal P(S)] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(S)\right| = 2^{\left| S \right|}.]

Content:
In other words, a finite set with cardinality [MATH: |S|] has [MATH: 2^{|S|}] subsets.

Content:
For example, for the set [MATH: S = \{ a,b,c \},] we have [MATH: |S| = 3,] and therefore

Content:
[MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(S)\right| = 2^{\left| S \right|} = 2^3 = 8.]

Content:
This tells us that [MATH: S] has [MATH: 8] subsets, and consequently, [MATH: \mathcal{P}(S)] has [MATH: 8] elements.

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{P}(S) = \big\{
\underbrace{\emptyset}_1,
\underbrace{ \{a\}}_2,
\underbrace{ \{b\}}_3,
\underbrace{ \{c\}}_4,
\underbrace{ \{ a,b \}}_5,
\underbrace{ \{ a,c \}}_6,
\underbrace{ \{ b,c \}}_7,
\underbrace{ \{ a,b,c \}}_8
\big\}]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- It's clear from our rule that if [MATH: S] is finite, then [MATH: \mathcal P(S)] is finite.
- It can be shown that if [MATH: S] is infinite, then [MATH: \mathcal P(S)] is also infinite.

Content:
We'll discuss power sets of infinite sets at the end of this lesson and in future lessons.

items.title: Computing the Cardinality of a Power Set

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: Y = \{ 1, \{ 3, 5 \}, 7, X \},] then what is [MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(Y)\right|?]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: Y = \{ 1, \{ 3, 5 \}, 7, X \},] then what is [MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(Y)\right|?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
For any set [MATH: Y,] we have [MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(Y)\right| = 2^{\left| Y \right|}.]

In this case, [MATH: \left| Y \right| = 4,] so we have [MATH: \left| \mathcal{P}(Y) \right| = 2^{\left| Y \right|} = 2^{4} = 16.]

Remember that [MATH: \{ 3,5 \}] is a single element in the set [MATH: Y.]

items.title: Determining Cardinality in More Advanced Cases

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: Y =\{\mu\}] and [MATH: Z =\{1,2\},] find [MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(Y\times Z))\right|.]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: Y =\{\mu\}] and [MATH: Z =\{1,2\},] find [MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(Y\times Z))\right|.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
For any set [MATH: S,] we have [MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(S)\right| = 2^{\left| S \right|}.] Also, [MATH: |S \times T| = |S| \cdot |T|.]

In our case,

[MATH: \left| Y \right| = 1, \qquad \left| Z \right| = 2.]

As a result,

[MATH: |P(Y × Z)||= 2^{|Y × Z|}; = 2^{|Y|⋅|Z|}; = 2^{1 ⋅ 2}; = 2^{2}; = 4.]

Therefore, we obtain

[MATH: |P(P(Y × Z))||= 2^{|P(Y × Z)|}; = 2^{4}; = 16.]

In this lesson, our primary focus was on power sets of finite sets. The definition of the power set of an infinite set mirrors that of finite sets. Namely, it comprises all possible subsets.

As we already understand, for finite sets, the size of power sets grows exponentially based on the size of the underlying set:

When dealing with power sets of infinite sets, the situation is more intricate.

Content:
For example, let's consider [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2,] the set containing all points on the Cartesian plane. What are the elements of the power set [MATH: \mathcal P(\mathbb R^2)?]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose [MATH: S] is a set. The power set of [MATH: S,] denoted [MATH: \mathcal{P}(S),] is the set containing every subset of [MATH: S,] including the empty set.

Content:
For example, let's find the power set of the set

Content:
[MATH: S = \{ 1,2,3 \}.]

Content:
To do this, we list out all the subsets of [MATH: S{:}]

Content:
- The subset containing no elements is [MATH: \emptyset.]
- The subsets containing [MATH: 1] element are [MATH: \{ 1 \},] [MATH: \{ 2 \},] and [MATH: \{ 3 \}.]
- The subsets containing [MATH: 2] elements are [MATH: \{ 1,2 \},] [MATH: \{ 1,3 \},] and [MATH: \{ 2,3 \}.]
- The subset containing [MATH: 3] elements is [MATH: S] itself: [MATH: \{ 1,2,3 \}.]

Content:
Now, let's put all these subsets together as elements of a single set. We get

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{P}(S) = \big\{ \emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{ 1,2 \}, \{ 1,3 \}, \{ 2,3 \}, \{ 1,2,3 \} \big\}.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Using a Tree Diagram

Content:
Another way to generate all the subsets of [MATH: S=\{ 1,2,3 \}] is using a tree diagram. We start off with the empty set [MATH: \{\}] and generate additional subsets of [MATH: S] by systematically inserting or excluding elements of [MATH: S.]

Content:
Let's go through the process.

Content:
- Start with the empty set [MATH: \{\}] at the root node of our tree. This is the parent node.
- Draw two branches pointing away from the parent node. The tip of each arrow gives a child node. Label one branch 'No' and the other 'Yes'.

[IMG: /graphics/b4a7a88ae1f90be541367655ad6fb2dc]
- We'll now write down a subset of [MATH: S] at each child node:

- At the child node (tip of the arrow) whose branch is labeled 'No,' we write down the parent node's set.
[MATH: \{\}]
- At the child node whose branch is labeled 'Yes,' we create a new set by inserting the first element of [MATH: S] into the parent node's set. This gives the following subset of [MATH: S{:}]
[MATH: \{1\}]
We now have the following diagram.

[IMG: /graphics/4259611c46a8ca9601625713bc12c483]

Content:
We repeat the process, setting the subsets found in the previous step as the new parent nodes.

Content:
- We start by considering the parent node [MATH: \{\}{:}]

- At the child node whose branch is labeled 'No', we write down the parent node's set.
[MATH: \{\}]
- At the child node whose branch is labeled 'Yes,' we create a new set by inserting the second element of [MATH: S] into the parent node's set. This gives the following subset of [MATH: S{:}]
[MATH: \{2\}]
We now have the following diagram.

[IMG: /graphics/8272d9581365eacdfa77a9cba1424918]
- Then, we consider the parent node [MATH: \{1\}{:}]

- At the child node whose branch is labeled 'No', we write down the parent node's set.
[MATH: \{1\}]
- At the child node whose branch is labeled 'Yes,' we create a new set by inserting the second element of [MATH: S] into the parent node's set. This gives the following subset of [MATH: S{:}]
[MATH: \{1,2\}]
We now have the following diagram.

[IMG: /graphics/664f7152d9215b771aee507f9a803926]
- Finally, we repeat the process for the new parent nodes [MATH: \{\}, \{2\}, \{1\},] and [MATH: \{1,2\}.]

Our final tree diagram looks as follows.

[IMG: /graphics/607b826c840be9e34912dfd04a3bcc43]

Content:
The final column lists all subsets of [MATH: S.]

Content:
[MATH: \emptyset = \{\},\quad \{1\},\quad \{2\},\quad \{3\},\quad \{ 1,2 \},\quad \{ 1,3 \},\quad \{ 2,3 \},\quad \{ 1,2,3 \}]

Content:
Finally then, we can write down [MATH: \mathcal P(S){:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{P}(S) = \big\{ \emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{ 1,2 \}, \{ 1,3 \}, \{ 2,3 \}, \{ 1,2,3 \} \big\}.]

---

Item 3 — Example: Listing the Elements in a Power Set

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: \mathcal{P}(A)] if [MATH: A = \{ 2, 4, \{ 8 \} \}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The power set of [MATH: A,] denoted [MATH: \mathcal{P}(A),] is the set that contains every possible subset of [MATH: A,] including the empty set [MATH: \emptyset.]

So, let's list all possible subsets of [MATH: A] using a tree diagram.

[IMG: /graphics/87c0e740ce1476af9e41cec575d50873]

According to our diagram, the subsets of [MATH: A] are
[MATH: \emptyset = \{\},\quad \{2\},\quad \{4\},\quad \{ \{8\} \}, \quad \{2, 4\},\quad \{2, \{8\}\},\quad \{4, \{8\}\},\quad\{2, 4, \{8\}\}.]

Therefore, we have
[MATH: \mathcal{P}(A) = \{\emptyset, \{2\}, \{4\}, \{\{8\}\}, \{2, 4\}, \{2, \{8\}\}, \{4, \{8\}\},\{2, 4, \{8\}\}\}.]

---

Item 7 — Tutorial: The Cardinality of a Power Set

Content:
Suppose we have a finite set [MATH: S] with cardinality [MATH: |S|.] Then, the cardinality of [MATH: \mathcal P(S)] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(S)\right| = 2^{\left| S \right|}.]

Content:
In other words, a finite set with cardinality [MATH: |S|] has [MATH: 2^{|S|}] subsets.

Content:
For example, for the set [MATH: S = \{ a,b,c \},] we have [MATH: |S| = 3,] and therefore

Content:
[MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(S)\right| = 2^{\left| S \right|} = 2^3 = 8.]

Content:
This tells us that [MATH: S] has [MATH: 8] subsets, and consequently, [MATH: \mathcal{P}(S)] has [MATH: 8] elements.

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{P}(S) = \big\{
\underbrace{\emptyset}_1,
\underbrace{ \{a\}}_2,
\underbrace{ \{b\}}_3,
\underbrace{ \{c\}}_4,
\underbrace{ \{ a,b \}}_5,
\underbrace{ \{ a,c \}}_6,
\underbrace{ \{ b,c \}}_7,
\underbrace{ \{ a,b,c \}}_8
\big\}]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- It's clear from our rule that if [MATH: S] is finite, then [MATH: \mathcal P(S)] is finite.
- It can be shown that if [MATH: S] is infinite, then [MATH: \mathcal P(S)] is also infinite.

Content:
We'll discuss power sets of infinite sets at the end of this lesson and in future lessons.

---

Item 8 — Example: Computing the Cardinality of a Power Set

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: Y = \{ 1, \{ 3, 5 \}, 7, X \},] then what is [MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(Y)\right|?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For any set [MATH: Y,] we have [MATH: \left|\mathcal{P}(Y)\right| = 2^{\left| Y \right|}.]

In this case, [MATH: \left| Y \right| = 4,] so we have
[MATH: \left| \mathcal{P}(Y) \right| = 2^{\left| Y \right|} = 2^{4} = 16.]

Remember that [MATH: \{ 3,5 \}] is a single element in the set [MATH: Y.]

Item 18 — Tutorial: Power Sets of Infinite Sets

Content:
In this lesson, our primary focus was on power sets of finite sets. The definition of the power set of an infinite set mirrors that of finite sets. Namely, it comprises all possible subsets.

Content:
As we already understand, for finite sets, the size of power sets grows exponentially based on the size of the underlying set:

Content:
[MATH: \big| \mathcal{P}(X) \big| = 2^{|X|}]

Content:
When dealing with power sets of infinite sets, the situation is more intricate.

Content:
For example, let's consider [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2,] the set containing all points on the Cartesian plane. What are the elements of the power set [MATH: \mathcal P(\mathbb R^2)?]

Content:
Any collection of points on the plane is a subset of [MATH: \mathbb R^2.] Such subsets can be visualized as black-and-white images on the plane, where points belonging to the subset are drawn in black, and points not belonging to the subset are represented in white.

Content:
For instance, each of the following images gives us a specific element of [MATH: \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^2){:}]
